title: Romulus founds Rome (legend)
summary: In the legend, twins Romulus and Remus, suckled by a she-wolf, found a city by the Tiber. Romulus kills his brother in a quarrel and names it after himself. 21 April 753 BC is the date later Roman scholars worked out.
significance: The story is myth, but archaeology does show huts on the Palatine Hill around this time. Romans celebrated the city's birthday on 21 April, and Rome still does.
questions: How much of the Romulus story is true?

title: The last king expelled; the Republic begins
summary: According to Livy, the king's son rapes a noblewoman, Lucretia, and the nobles rise up and drive out King Tarquinius Superbus. In place of a king, Romans elect two consuls each year.
significance: Romans hated the word 'king' for centuries afterwards. Even the emperors avoided it.

title: The Twelve Tables: Rome's first written laws
summary: After pressure from the plebeians, ordinary citizens shut out of power, a commission writes Rome's laws down and displays them in the Forum for everyone to see.
significance: The start of Roman law, which still shapes legal systems across Europe and beyond.

title: Rome conquers Veii
summary: After a siege that tradition says lasted ten years, Rome captures its big Etruscan neighbour, just 15 km away, and roughly doubles its territory.
significance: Rome's first big conquest, and the moment it outgrew its neighbours.

title: The Gauls sack Rome
summary: A Gallic army routs the Romans at the River Allia and sacks the city. Legend says the sacred geese on the Capitol woke the defenders in time to save it, and that the Gallic chief Brennus threw his sword on the scales while the Romans paid a ransom, crying 'woe to the vanquished'.
significance: Rome was not sacked again for 800 years. The trauma made it build stronger walls and a tougher army.

title: Rome dissolves the Latin League
summary: Rome beats its rebellious Latin allies and splits them up, giving some full citizenship, some partial citizenship, and binding each one to Rome separately.
significance: This flexible system of alliances and citizenship was the secret of how Rome absorbed Italy.

title: Humiliation at the Caudine Forks
summary: The Samnites, tough hill peoples of the Apennines, trap a whole Roman army in a mountain pass. Each soldier is forced to walk under a yoke of spears in surrender.
significance: A byword for humiliation. Rome tore up the peace and kept fighting the Samnites for decades.

title: Battle of Sentinum
summary: Samnites, Gauls, Etruscans and Umbrians join forces against Rome. Rome wins the biggest battle Italy had yet seen. Consul Decius Mus sacrifices himself in a ritual vow to win the gods' favour.
significance: It decided who would rule Italy.

title: Pyrrhus and his 'Pyrrhic victories'
summary: The Greek city of Tarentum calls in King Pyrrhus of Epirus, with elephants and a professional army. He beats the Romans twice but loses so many men he says, according to Plutarch, that one more such victory would finish him.
significance: Rome learned it could lose battles and still win wars by out-lasting its enemies.

title: Tarentum falls: Rome rules Italy
summary: With Pyrrhus gone home, Tarentum surrenders. Rome now controls the whole Italian peninsula south of the River Po.
significance: Italy's manpower, organised through Rome's alliances, would make Rome almost unbeatable.

title: War with Carthage begins
summary: Rome sends an army across to Sicily, starting the first of three wars with Carthage, the great sea power of the western Mediterranean.
significance: The start of Rome's overseas empire.

seeAlso.label: Follow it in Rome v Carthage

title: Sicily: Rome's first province
summary: Victory at sea forces Carthage out of Sicily. Rome makes it its first province, governed by a Roman magistrate and paying taxes in grain.
significance: Provinces, governors and taxes: the template for the whole empire.

seeAlso.label: The Aegates Islands in Rome v Carthage

title: Hannibal destroys a Roman army at Cannae
summary: Hannibal, who has crossed the Alps with elephants, surrounds and annihilates the largest army Rome has ever fielded.
significance: Rome's darkest day. It refused to make peace, and won the war fourteen years later.

seeAlso.label: Watch Cannae unfold in Rome v Carthage

title: Scipio beats Hannibal at Zama
summary: Scipio takes the war to Africa and defeats Hannibal. Carthage loses Spain and its navy.
significance: Rome is now the only great power in the western Mediterranean.

title: Battle of Pydna: the end of Macedon
summary: The flexible Roman legion breaks the Macedonian phalanx, the formation of Alexander the Great's heirs, on rough ground. King Perseus is captured and his kingdom abolished.
significance: The Greek east would now take orders from Rome. Polybius, who was taken to Rome as a hostage after this war, set out to explain how Rome conquered the world so fast.

title: Carthage and Corinth destroyed
summary: In a single year, Roman armies raze two of the greatest cities of the Mediterranean: Carthage in Africa and Corinth in Greece.
significance: Africa and Macedonia become provinces. Roman historians later saw this as the moment success began to corrupt Rome.

seeAlso.label: The end of Carthage in Rome v Carthage

title: Tiberius Gracchus murdered
summary: Tribune Tiberius Gracchus pushes through a law to share public land with poor citizens. Senators club him and hundreds of his supporters to death. The same year the king of Pergamon leaves his kingdom to Rome in his will.
significance: The first political killing in Rome for centuries. Violence was now part of Roman politics, and it never went away.

title: Marius crushes the Cimbri and Teutones
summary: Migrating Germanic tribes have destroyed several Roman armies. Gaius Marius, consul five years running, rebuilds the army and wipes them out in 102 and 101 BC.
significance: Marius recruited the landless poor, who looked to their general rather than the state for pay and land. Armies loyal to generals would destroy the Republic.

title: The Social War: Italy rises
summary: Rome's Italian allies, who fight in its wars but cannot vote, rebel and set up their own state with its capital at Corfinium. Rome wins the war but gives way on citizenship.
significance: By 88 BC almost every free man in Italy south of the Po was a Roman citizen.

title: Sulla marches on Rome and becomes dictator
summary: Having already marched his army on Rome once, Sulla wins a civil war and makes himself dictator. He posts lists of enemies who can be killed for a reward, and their property seized.
significance: Sulla resigned and retired, but he had shown everyone how to take Rome by force.

title: Spartacus defeated
place: Via Appia, from Capua to Rome
stat: About 6,000 survivors crucified along the Via Appia
summary: The gladiator Spartacus broke out of a training school at Capua in 73 BC, and his slave army beat several Roman forces. Crassus finally crushes it.
significance: The crosses lined the road from Capua to Rome as a warning. Crassus and Pompey, rivals in the victory, both became consuls.

title: Pompey reorganises the East
summary: Pompey defeats King Mithridates of Pontus, ends the Seleucid kingdom, makes Syria a province and captures Jerusalem, entering the Temple's holy of holies.
significance: Rome's border now reached the Euphrates, face to face with Parthia.

title: Caesar wins Gaul at Alesia
summary: Julius Caesar traps the Gallic leader Vercingetorix in the hill town of Alesia and builds two rings of walls, one to keep the Gauls in and one to keep a huge relief army out. He beats both.
significance: Gaul, roughly modern France and Belgium, became Roman. Caesar was now rich, famous and commanded a devoted army.
questions: Why did Caesar build two walls?

title: Caesar crosses the Rubicon
summary: Ordered by the Senate to give up his army, Caesar leads it across the little river that marked the edge of his province. 'The die is cast,' he is said to have said. Civil war.
significance: Crossing the Rubicon still means passing the point of no return.

title: Caesar beats Pompey at Pharsalus
summary: Caesar defeats the Senate's army under Pompey, even though he is outnumbered. Pompey flees to Egypt, where he is murdered as he steps ashore.
significance: Caesar is master of the Roman world. In Egypt he backs Cleopatra for the throne.

title: The Ides of March
summary: Made dictator for life, Caesar is stabbed 23 times by a group of senators led by Brutus and Cassius, at the foot of Pompey's statue.
significance: The assassins wanted to save the Republic. Instead they set off another round of civil wars, won by Caesar's adopted heir Octavian.
questions: Why did Brutus join the plot?

title: Battle of Actium
summary: Octavian's fleet, commanded by Agrippa, beats Mark Antony and Cleopatra. The next year both kill themselves in Alexandria, and Egypt becomes Octavian's personal province.
significance: The last civil war of the Republic. One man now controlled every army.

title: Octavian becomes Augustus
summary: Octavian claims to 'restore the Republic' and hands power back to the Senate, which promptly gives most of it back and names him Augustus, 'the revered one'.
significance: Historians date the Roman Empire from here. Augustus kept the old offices and called himself 'first citizen', but he was a monarch in all but name.

title: Disaster in the Teutoburg Forest
summary: Arminius, a German chief trained in the Roman army, leads three legions under Varus into an ambush in forest and swamp. All three are wiped out.
significance: Augustus reportedly cried 'Varus, give me back my legions!' Rome gave up on conquering Germany beyond the Rhine.

title: Claudius invades Britain
summary: Emperor Claudius sends four legions across the Channel, and turns up himself, with elephants, to see the capture of Camulodunum (Colchester).
significance: Britain was Roman for almost four centuries. London was founded a few years later.

title: The Great Fire of Rome
summary: A fire starting near the Circus Maximus burns for six days and destroys much of the city. Nero blames the Christians and has many put to death.
significance: The story that Nero fiddled while Rome burned is a later legend, but he did use the cleared land for his vast Golden House.

title: Jerusalem and its Temple destroyed
summary: Four years into a Jewish revolt, Titus, son of the new emperor Vespasian, takes Jerusalem after a long siege and burns the Temple.
significance: A turning point in Jewish history. The treasure helped pay for the Colosseum, and the Arch of Titus in Rome still shows the Temple menorah being carried in triumph.

title: Vesuvius buries Pompeii
summary: The volcano erupts and buries Pompeii and Herculaneum under ash and pumice. Pliny the Elder dies trying to rescue people by boat; his nephew writes an eyewitness account.
significance: The buried towns are the best snapshot we have of ordinary Roman life. The traditional date is 24 August, but recent finds point to October.
wiki: Eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD

title: The Colosseum opens
summary: Emperor Titus opens the Flavian Amphitheatre with 100 days of games. It could hold around 50,000 spectators for gladiator fights, wild animal hunts and executions.
significance: Bread and circuses: free food and spectacle kept the city's huge population on the emperor's side.

title: The empire at its greatest extent
place: From Scotland to the Persian Gulf
summary: Trajan has conquered Dacia (modern Romania) and briefly takes Armenia and Mesopotamia down to the Persian Gulf. He dies in 117 on the way home; his successor Hadrian gives up the eastern conquests at once.
significance: Roughly 5 million square kilometres and perhaps 60 million people. It never got bigger.

title: Hadrian's Wall
summary: Hadrian, who spends much of his reign touring the provinces, orders a wall 73 miles long across northern Britain.
significance: The empire stopped expanding and started defending fixed frontiers.

title: Death of Marcus Aurelius
summary: The philosopher-emperor, who wrote his Meditations in army camps on the Danube while fighting Germanic tribes, dies on campaign. His son Commodus takes over.
significance: The historian Cassius Dio wrote that the empire now fell 'from a kingdom of gold to one of iron and rust'.

title: Citizenship for all free men
summary: Emperor Caracalla grants Roman citizenship to almost every free man in the empire.
significance: Being 'Roman' was no longer about Rome or Italy. Cassius Dio claimed the real aim was to collect more inheritance tax.

title: The Crisis of the Third Century begins
summary: Soldiers murder Emperor Severus Alexander on the Rhine. Over the next 50 years more than 20 emperors claim the throne, most of them killed by their own troops.
significance: Civil war, plague, Persian and Gothic invasions and a collapsing currency, all at once.

title: Emperor Valerian captured by Persia
summary: The Persian king Shapur I defeats and captures Emperor Valerian, the only Roman emperor ever taken prisoner. He dies in captivity. The same year Gaul, Britain and Spain break away as the Gallic Empire.
significance: Shapur carved the scene into a cliff at Naqsh-e Rostam in Iran. It is still there.

title: Queen Zenobia's Palmyrene Empire
summary: Zenobia, ruling the desert trading city of Palmyra for her young son, seizes Egypt and much of the Roman east.
significance: For a few years the empire was in three pieces: the Gallic Empire in the west, Palmyra in the east, and Rome in the middle.

title: Aurelian, 'Restorer of the World'
summary: In four years Emperor Aurelian crushes Palmyra, takes Zenobia captive, and wins back the Gallic Empire. He also builds new walls around Rome itself.
significance: The empire was whole again, but Rome needed walls. Much of the Aurelian Wall still stands.

title: Diocletian's rule of four
summary: Diocletian decides the empire is too big for one man and shares power among four emperors, two senior and two junior, each with his own capital near a frontier.
significance: Rome itself was no longer where emperors lived. Diocletian also led the last great persecution of Christians.

title: Constantine at the Milvian Bridge
summary: Before battle, Constantine has a vision of a Christian sign and is told 'in this sign, conquer'. He defeats his rival Maxentius, who drowns in the Tiber.
significance: The next year the Edict of Milan grants Christians freedom of worship. Within 80 years Christianity was the state religion.

title: Constantinople founded
summary: Constantine refounds the Greek city of Byzantium as a new, Christian capital on the straits between Europe and Asia, and names it after himself.
significance: Constantinople would be the capital of the Roman Empire in the east until 1453.

title: Goths kill Emperor Valens at Adrianople
summary: Goths fleeing the Huns were let into the empire, then mistreated by Roman officials until they revolted. At Adrianople their cavalry and infantry destroy the eastern army, and Valens is killed.
significance: The Goths could not be driven out. From now on, Germanic peoples settled inside the empire as semi-independent allies.

title: The empire divides for good
summary: Theodosius, the last emperor to rule both halves, dies. The empire passes to his two young sons: Arcadius in the East and Honorius in the West.
significance: Officially still one empire, in practice two, and the East was the richer half.

title: Vandals, Alans and Suebi cross the Rhine
summary: With frontier troops pulled back to defend Italy, a great mass of peoples crosses the Rhine, by tradition on the last day of 406, and spreads through Gaul and on into Spain.
significance: The western provinces would never be fully recovered.

title: Britain left to defend itself
summary: With Roman troops withdrawn to fight usurpers on the continent, the British cities are told, according to the historian Zosimus, to look to their own defence.
significance: Roman Britain faded away. Within two centuries, Anglo-Saxon kingdoms held most of what would become England.
wiki: End of Roman rule in Britain

title: Alaric's Goths sack Rome
summary: After years of failed negotiations with the western court, safe behind the marshes at Ravenna, the Visigoth leader Alaric lets his army loot Rome for three days.
significance: The first sack of Rome by a foreign enemy in 800 years shocked the Roman world. Augustine wrote The City of God partly in reply.

title: The Vandals take Carthage
summary: King Gaiseric's Vandals, who had crossed from Spain to Africa ten years earlier, seize Carthage and the western empire's richest provinces.
significance: Losing Africa's grain and taxes was a body blow to the West. The Vandals also took its fleet.

title: Attila stopped on the Catalaunian Plains
summary: Attila's Huns invade Gaul. The Roman general Aetius, allied with the Visigoths, fights him to a standstill in one of the biggest battles of the age.
significance: Often called the last victory of the western empire. Attila died two years later and his empire fell apart.

title: The Vandals sack Rome
summary: Sailing from Carthage, Gaiseric's Vandals loot Rome for two weeks, carrying off treasure and captives, including the empress and her daughters.
significance: It gave us the word 'vandalism', though the sack was more orderly than the name suggests.

title: The last western emperor deposed
summary: Odoacer, commander of the Germanic troops in Italy, deposes the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus and sends the imperial regalia to Constantinople, saying the West no longer needs an emperor of its own.
significance: The traditional end of the Roman Empire in the West. The East, ruled from Constantinople, lasted until 1453.
wiki: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
questions: Why did the western empire fall?
Did people at the time notice it had fallen?
